discussion_comments.comment_body:
Agreed, and fixed in ba90629.

Measured first, on a two-commit fixture whose second commit replaces a 1 MiB blob with 20 MiB of incompressible data (macOS 15, Python 3.14.5, git 2.50.1). `git diff --binary` emitted a **27.1 MiB** patch, and `committed_diff_content_digest` peaked at **88.9 MiB RSS** against a 27.4 MiB floor — so the buffered patch really is the whole difference.

`committed_diff_content_digest` now builds the digest first and streams the patch into it through a new `git_digest_field`, which spools Git's stdout into a private temporary file, takes the value length from `os.fstat`, and hashes the file in 1 MiB chunks. Same fixture, same process shape: **88.9 MiB → 27.4 MiB peak RSS**, a floor set by the interpreter plus the hashing chunk rather than by the patch.

Streaming straight from the pipe into `hashlib` is not available: `update_digest_field` writes an 8-byte big-endian *value length* before the value, so the total byte count is part of the hashed material and has to be known before any content is hashed. A second `git diff` purely to count bytes would double the work and would not be atomic. Spooling keeps one Git invocation and gets the length from `fstat`.

Digest stability matters more than usual here, because the revalidation added for your other comment on this PR compares recorded digests against freshly computed ones — a changed digest would read as changed reviewed content. Buffered and streaming were run in separate processes over the same fixtures and agreed on every one:

| fixture | buffered == streaming |
| --- | --- |
| empty range | identical `1d74df0bc5da366e…` |
| text diff | identical `25e510ab75f7ee0d…` |
| 64 KiB binary diff | identical `3a78c1c5207e0c36…` |
| rename | identical `03e6430eaef2bc18…` |
| mode change | identical `cb87a9351fcbe0cc…` |
| root commit vs empty tree | identical `77315e8f791716cc…` |
| 20 MiB binary diff (27.1 MiB patch) | identical `7908fcf6b0ea2eff…` |

The empty range reproduces `1d74df0b…`, which is the hardcoded `clean_worktree_content_digest()` sentinel — the framing is unchanged down to that constant. Failure behaviour is unchanged too: against an unresolvable base, buffered and streaming both exit 1 with `Could not snapshot the selected committed changes.`

`git_command` gained a keyword-only `stdout` so the streaming path reuses the existing environment scrubbing and `core.fsmonitor=false` hardening instead of building its own command, and `capture_output=True` became the equivalent explicit `stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE`. `git_bytes` is untouched and still serves its many small callers.

**Relationship to #256.** That PR fixes the same defect on the other digest path — `worktree_content_digest_for_context`, the working-tree diff — and branches from `ea19f24`, where `committed_diff_content_digest` does not exist yet. So neither PR covers the other's call site: #256 streams the working-tree patch, this one streams the committed patch. To keep that from becoming a conflict, `git_digest_field` and the `git_command` signature change here are byte-for-byte identical to #256's, verified by diffing the two files. Whichever lands first, the other's helper merges as an identical addition and only its own call site remains.

Covered by `tests-ts/scan-recovery.test.ts`, `streams the committed patch instead of buffering it`. Rather than assert on memory, which would be flaky, it wraps `workbench_target.git_bytes` in a spy, runs `committed_diff_content_digest` over a changed binary, and requires that no `diff` invocation went through it — `git_bytes` *is* `capture_output=True`, so any diff call through it is a buffered patch. It then recomputes the digest through the buffered `git_bytes` + `update_digest_field` pair the streaming path replaced and requires the two values to be equal, so the framing cannot drift.

Measured, from `sdk/typescript`: full suite **743 pass / 5 skip / 0 fail**. With `workbench_target.py` reverted to its previous state, **742 pass / 5 skip / 1 fail** — that test. `types` and `format` clean; both changed Python modules compile under `python3 -m py_compile`.
